pages.text:
Week 3 — Database Normalisation.

Normalisation is the process of organising columns and tables to reduce redundancy. Redundancy causes update anomalies: the same fact stored twice can be changed in one place and not the other.

A functional dependency A -> B means that for any given value of A there is exactly one value of B. In a student table, student_id -> student_name is a functional dependency: one id, one name.

First normal form (1NF) requires that every column holds a single atomic value. A column containing 'maths, physics, chemistry' violates 1NF; those belong in three rows of a separate table.

Second normal form (2NF) requires 1NF plus no partial dependency: no non-key column may depend on only part of a composite primary key. If the key is (student_id, course_code) then course_title depends on course_code alone, which is a partial dependency and must move to a course table.

Third normal form (3NF) requires 2NF plus no transitive dependency: no non-key column may depend on another non-key column. If student_id -> postcode and postcode -> city, then city depends on the key only through postcode. That is transitive, and city belongs in a postcode table.

In practice most operational schemas are normalised to 3NF and stop there. Going further can cost more in joins than it saves in storage.
